    Overview

    Questions

    • What is precision agriculture?
    • Why is spatial variability important in farming?
    • How can GPS, GIS, and satellite imagery support farm management?
    • How can we create a basic digital farm map?

    Objectives

    By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:

    1. Define precision agriculture and explain its objectives.
    2. Identify common precision agriculture technologies.
    3. Distinguish between points, lines, polygons, and raster data.
    4. Locate an agricultural field using Google Earth Pro.
    5. Create and export a digital farm boundary.
    6. Explain how spatial information supports agricultural decisions.

    1. Introduction

    Precision agriculture (PA) is a farm management approach that uses spatial, temporal, and other data to support management decisions.

    Its purpose is to account for variability within agricultural fields and improve the efficiency of agricultural inputs and operations.

    Traditional farming often applies uniform treatments across a field.

    Precision agriculture allows farmers to make location-specific decisions based on measured conditions.

    Example: Fertilizer Application

    Consider a wheat field in Sulaymaniyah.

    Soil fertility may vary across the field:

    • Zone A: Low nitrogen availability
    • Zone B: Moderate nitrogen availability
    • Zone C: High nitrogen availability

    Applying the same fertilizer rate everywhere may be inefficient.

    Using soil sampling, GPS, and GIS, the farmer can create a fertility map and develop different fertilizer recommendations for each zone.

    Callout

    Key Concept

    Precision agriculture does not simply mean using advanced machinery.

    It means collecting relevant data, analyzing variability, making informed decisions, and evaluating the results.

    2. Important Precision Agriculture Technologies

    Technology Agricultural Application
    GPS/GNSS Field positioning and machinery guidance
    GIS Agricultural mapping and spatial analysis
    Remote sensing Monitoring crop and land conditions
    Satellite imagery Vegetation and land-cover monitoring
    Drones (UAVs) High-resolution field observations
    Soil sensors Measuring soil conditions
    Weather stations Monitoring agricultural weather
    Variable-rate technology Adjusting agricultural inputs by location

    Photo: GNSS guidance equipment

    Figure 1. A real agricultural GNSS guidance display and receiver. This is an example of positioning equipment, not a screenshot of a field map. Photograph: Mr. Justice USA, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Image reproduced unchanged.

    Look closely: Which component displays information to the tractor operator, and which component receives satellite navigation signals? How could knowing a tractor’s location reduce missed passes or overlapping applications?

    3. Understanding Spatial Data

    GIS commonly uses vector and raster data.

    Vector Data

    Vector data represents geographic objects using:

    Points

    Examples: - Soil sampling locations - Irrigation wells - Weather stations

    Lines

    Examples: - Irrigation pipelines - Tractor routes - Farm access roads

    Polygons

    Examples: - Agricultural field boundaries - Irrigation zones - Soil management zones

    Visual guide: Points, lines, and polygons

    Figure 2. Vector data illustrated by wells (points), a river (line), and a lake (polygon). Illustration: M. W. Toews, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Image reproduced unchanged.

    Apply this to farming: Replace the well with a soil-sampling location, the river with an irrigation pipe or tractor route, and the lake with a field boundary.

    Raster Data

    Raster data consists of a grid of cells.

    Examples: - Satellite images - NDVI maps - Digital elevation models - Temperature maps

    Visual guide: Vector versus raster representation

    Figure 3. The same area represented by vector and raster models. Illustration: Gegot, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Image reproduced unchanged.

    A vector polygon follows connected boundary vertices. A raster covers space with individual grid cells, so an edge is represented at the raster’s cell resolution.

    Watch: Vector versus raster in GIS

    This short video introduces points, lines, polygons, and raster grids. Watch before attempting Exercise 1.

    Video: Vector vs. Raster Data Explained | Beginner-Friendly GIS Course, Atlas (2025), via YouTube. Video remains hosted by its creator. If the embedded player is unavailable, use the linked YouTube page.

    Challenge

    Exercise 1: Identify the Data Type

    Identify the most suitable GIS data representation for each feature:

    1. An agricultural weather station
    2. A tractor travel path
    3. A wheat field boundary
    4. A satellite-derived NDVI image
    1. Weather station: Point
    2. Tractor path: Line
    3. Wheat field boundary: Polygon
    4. NDVI image: Raster

    4. Practical Activity: Digital Farm Mapping

    Software: Google Earth Pro

    Study area: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq

    Estimated practical time: 20 minutes

    Step 1: Open Google Earth Pro

    1. Launch Google Earth Pro.
    2. Enter “Sulaymaniyah, Iraq” into the search box.
    3. Navigate toward an agricultural area.
    4. Zoom in until agricultural field boundaries are visible.

    Step 2: Observe the Landscape

    Identify at least three of the following features:

    • Agricultural fields
    • Roads
    • Irrigation canals
    • Orchards
    • Buildings
    • Water resources

    Record your observations.

    Watch before digitizing: Drawing a polygon in Google Earth Pro

    This walkthrough shows how to create a polygon, edit its vertices, and correct an outline. It demonstrates the same type of polygon students will use for their training-field boundary.

    Video: Google Earth Pro | How to Create and Edit Polygons, Sabankou Kpatadoa (2023), via YouTube. Polygon creation begins at 0:13; editing begins around 3:46. Video remains hosted by its creator.

    Step 3: Create a Farm Boundary

    1. Select a visible agricultural field.
    2. Click Add > Polygon.
    3. Enter the name Training Farm 01.
    4. Click around the boundary of the selected field.
    5. Choose a suitable outline color.
    6. Click OK to save the polygon.

    Step 4: Inspect the Boundary

    1. Right-click your polygon.
    2. Select Properties.
    3. Open the Measurements tab.
    4. Inspect the perimeter and area.
    5. Record the area in hectares, if available.

    Step 5: Add a Point

    1. Click Add > Placemark.
    2. Place the marker on an identifiable feature.
    3. Name the marker Observation Point 01.
    4. Record its latitude and longitude.

    Step 6: Export the Data

    1. Create a folder in the Places panel.
    2. Move the farm polygon and observation point into it.
    3. Right-click the folder.
    4. Choose Save Place As.
    5. Export it as a KMZ file.

    Suggested filename:

    Lecture01_Farm_Observation.kmz

    Caution

    Important Note

    The training field is selected for educational purposes.

    Google Earth imagery is not necessarily current, and visually identified boundaries should not be treated as legally surveyed property boundaries.

    5. Guided Discussion

    Challenge

    Exercise 2: Why Does Location Matter?

    Two soil samples from the same agricultural field have different nitrogen concentrations.

    Question: Why might a farmer use different fertilizer rates in these locations?

    Different soil nitrogen levels may indicate different fertilizer requirements.

    The farmer can use georeferenced soil sampling results and GIS analysis to identify management zones.

    However, fertilizer recommendations should also consider crop requirements, soil test interpretation, expected yield, and other relevant agronomic factors.

    Challenge

    Exercise 3: Choose the Appropriate Technology

    Select the most appropriate technology for each task.

    1. Measuring the position of a tractor
    2. Producing a vegetation index from satellite imagery
    3. Creating a digital soil sampling map
    4. Automatically changing fertilizer application rates
    1. GNSS/GPS
    2. Satellite remote sensing
    3. GIS combined with georeferenced soil observations
    4. Variable-rate application equipment and a prescription or control system

    6. Student Assignment

    Assignment Title

    Creating a Basic Agricultural Field Map

    Students must create a digital agricultural map using Google Earth Pro.

    Required Outputs

    1. One agricultural field boundary polygon
    2. At least two point markers
    3. A screenshot showing the mapped features
    4. A KMZ file containing the mapped features
    5. A short written explanation of the map and its agricultural relevance

    Submission Filename

    Lecture01_StudentID.kmz

    Assessment Rubric

    Assessment Criterion Marks
    Correct field boundary 3
    Two observation points 2
    Correct KMZ export 2
    Map screenshot 1
    Agricultural explanation 2
    Total 10

    Submit the files through the submission method specified by your lecturer.

    7. Further Reading

    • QGIS Official Website
    • Google Earth
    • NASA Earthdata
    • FAO Geospatial Information

    Key Points
    • Precision agriculture uses data to support location-specific farm management.
    • Agricultural fields may contain significant spatial variability.
    • GPS/GNSS provides geographic positioning.
    • GIS supports the storage, visualization, and analysis of spatial information.
    • Points, lines, polygons, and rasters are fundamental GIS data structures.
    • Google Earth Pro can create and export basic agricultural maps.
    • KML and KMZ files can be used to exchange geographic features.

    Content from Lecture 2: GIS Fundamentals and Coordinate Systems

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How does a GIS store locations and their attributes?
    • What is the difference between latitude and longitude?
    • Why do EPSG:4326 and EPSG:32638 use different coordinate units?
    • How can Google Earth Pro show decimal degrees and UTM coordinates?

    Objectives

    By the end of this lesson, students should be able to:

    1. Explain the role of geometry, attributes and coordinate reference systems in GIS.
    2. Read latitude and longitude and convert degrees-minutes-seconds to decimal degrees.
    3. Distinguish geographic coordinates from projected metre-based coordinates.
    4. Identify WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) and WGS 84 / UTM Zone 38N (EPSG:32638).
    5. Record two agricultural observations in Google Earth Pro and export a KMZ file.
    6. Explain the difference between changing coordinate display and reprojecting GIS data.

    1. What does GIS store?

    A Geographic Information System (GIS) links where something is (geometry) with what it is (attributes). A record also needs a coordinate reference system, or CRS, so software can interpret its numeric position correctly.

    For example, one agricultural observation can contain:

    Element Example
    Geometry Point
    Latitude 35.5600° N
    Longitude 45.4300° E
    Attribute Soil observation
    CRS WGS 84 / EPSG:4326

    The coordinates above are illustrative, not survey measurements of a specific field.

    A GIS may combine points (soil samples), lines (irrigation pipes), polygons (field boundaries) and rasters (satellite imagery or elevation).

    2. Latitude and longitude

    Figure 1. Latitude and longitude on Earth. Original illustration by Djexplo on Wikimedia Commons, dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. Unmodified.

    Latitude measures angular position north or south of the Equator (0° latitude). Longitude measures angular position east or west of the Prime Meridian (0° longitude).

    • Geographic latitude ranges from -90° to +90°.
    • Longitude is commonly represented between -180° and +180°.
    • North and east values are positive in signed decimal-degree notation; south and west values are negative.

    Figure 2. Latitude and longitude angles for one point on Earth’s surface. Original diagram by Brews ohare, vector version by CheChe on Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Unmodified.

    Exercise: Reading a position

    An illustrative position near Sulaymaniyah is 35.5600° N, 45.4300° E.

    • Which number is latitude? 35.5600
    • Which number is longitude? 45.4300
    • In which hemispheres is the point? Northern and Eastern
    Challenge

    Quick check: Coordinate order

    A CSV has columns called `longitude` and `latitude`. When importing into QGIS as a point layer, which should be the X and Y fields?

    For this CSV, select X = longitude and Y = latitude, and set the source geographic CRS to EPSG:4326. Do not confuse the column order used in some web APIs with the X/Y fields in the QGIS importer.

    3. Decimal degrees and degrees-minutes-seconds

    The same position can be expressed using different formats:

    • Decimal degrees (DD): 35.5000° N
    • Degrees, minutes, seconds (DMS): 35° 30′ 00″ N

    Convert DMS to decimal degrees:

    `DD = degrees + minutes/60 + seconds/3600`

    For a south or west position, apply a negative sign to the absolute converted value.

    Challenge

    Practice: DMS conversion

    Convert 35° 30′ 00″ N and 45° 26′ 00″ E to decimal degrees.

    Latitude: 35 + 30/60 = 35.5000° N.

    Longitude: 45 + 26/60 = 45.4333° E (rounded to four decimal places).

    4. Geographic CRS versus projected CRS

    A geographic CRS describes locations with angular coordinates such as latitude and longitude. WGS 84 geographic coordinates use EPSG:4326, with degrees as units.

    A projected CRS represents the curved Earth on a flat coordinate plane. Many projected coordinate systems use metres for X and Y.

    Attribute WGS 84 geographic WGS 84 / UTM Zone 38N
    EPSG code 4326 32638
    Typical coordinates Latitude, longitude Easting, northing
    Coordinate units Degrees Metres
    Use in this course Recording positions Local field measurements and mapped analysis
    Callout

    Important: Assigning a CRS is not the same as reprojecting

    Assigning a source CRS tells QGIS what the existing numbers mean. Reprojecting transforms those numbers into another CRS. Changing the display format in Google Earth Pro only changes how coordinates are shown; it does not mean the exported placemark has become a projected UTM dataset.

    Watch: Coordinate reference systems in QGIS

    The original video below demonstrates multiple GIS layers using different CRSs and how QGIS displays them together using on-the-fly reprojection.

    Video: Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS) and QGIS, GIS - Tools to understand the world, 2024. Video hosted and owned by its YouTube creator.

    5. How UTM zones work

    The Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) system divides most of Earth’s land areas into 60 longitudinal zones, typically 6 degrees wide. Zones are numbered from west to east. Coordinates use a zone, hemisphere and metric easting and northing.

    Figure 3. Original UTM zone world map by cmglee, STyx, Wikialine and Goran tek-en on Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Unmodified; irregular zones are highlighted in the original map.

    Sulaymaniyah is in UTM Zone 38N. The regular longitudinal span of Zone 38 is 42°E–48°E, and its central meridian is 45°E. A useful projected reference for many local agricultural mapping tasks is EPSG:32638.

    Challenge

    Exercise: Choose the correct CRS

    You have coordinates for a wheat-field boundary near Sulaymaniyah. You want to calculate its approximate area in square metres. Which is the more suitable choice for a local planar area calculation?

    A. WGS 84 geographic, EPSG:4326
    B. WGS 84 / UTM Zone 38N, EPSG:32638

    B. EPSG:32638 uses metres and is well suited for many local mapping tasks near Sulaymaniyah. It is still important to check source accuracy and field digitization quality; no map projection eliminates those errors.

    6. Guided practical: Show DD and UTM in Google Earth Pro

    Software: Google Earth Pro on Windows
    Duration: About 30–35 minutes
    Study area: Agricultural landscape near Sulaymaniyah

    Step 1 — Navigate to a field

    1. Launch Google Earth Pro.
    2. Search for `Sulaymaniyah, Iraq`.
    3. Navigate to a visible agricultural area outside the urban centre.
    4. Observe roads, fields and orchard blocks; select two illustrative observation locations.

    Step 2 — Set coordinate display to decimal degrees

    1. Select Tools → Options → 3D View.
    2. Under Show Lat/Long, choose Decimal Degrees.
    3. Click Apply or OK.
    4. Move the mouse over the map to observe the position display, or open a new placemark to inspect its location.

    Watch: Changing coordinate formats in Google Earth Pro

    This YouTube walkthrough specifically covers latitude/longitude, UTM format and measurement-unit settings.

    Video: How to Change Units & Coordinate System in Google Earth Pro, John Okello, 2023. Video hosted and owned by its YouTube creator.

    Step 3 — Create two placemarks

    1. Select Add → Placemark.
    2. Move the placemark to your first observation position.
    3. Name it `Observation_A` and record latitude and longitude.
    4. Repeat for a second point named `Observation_B`.
    5. Save the points in a folder named `Lecture02_Coordinates` in the Places panel.

    Step 4 — Inspect the UTM display

    1. Reopen Tools → Options → 3D View.
    2. Change Show Lat/Long to Universal Transverse Mercator.
    3. For each placemark, inspect the displayed UTM zone, easting and northing.
    4. Record the results in the following table.
    Observation Latitude (°) Longitude (°) UTM zone Easting (m) Northing (m)
    Observation_A Student reading Student reading Student reading Student reading Student reading
    Observation_B Student reading Student reading Student reading Student reading Student reading

    Step 5 — Export and verify

    1. Right-click the folder `Lecture02_Coordinates`.
    2. Choose Save Place As and export `Lecture02_Coordinates.kmz`.
    3. Open that saved KMZ to confirm that both placemarks are present.
    4. Keep your coordinate-recording table and a screenshot of both markers.
    Caution

    Do not confuse display format with stored coordinates

    KML/KMZ geographic positions are conventionally stored as longitude, latitude (and optional altitude) using WGS 84. Showing UTM in Google Earth does not change that internal geographic representation. The KMZ is a useful teaching file, not survey-certified land data.

    7. Optional QGIS comparison

    If QGIS is already installed:

    1. Create a new QGIS project.
    2. Drag `Lecture02_Coordinates.kmz` into QGIS, choosing a suitable vector layer if prompted.
    3. Inspect the point layer’s CRS.
    4. Set the project CRS to EPSG:32638 and note how the coordinates shown in the QGIS status area change.
    5. Explain why changing the project CRS does not automatically rewrite the original KMZ.
    6. If asked to create projected data, use Export → Save Features As and select EPSG:32638 for a new GeoPackage output.

    8. Student assignment and rubric

    Submit:

    • `Lecture02_Coordinates.kmz` containing both named observation points.
    • One screenshot of the two locations in Google Earth Pro.
    • The completed decimal-degree and UTM coordinate table.
    • A 100–150 word explanation comparing EPSG:4326 and EPSG:32638.
    • A short note explaining image-based location uncertainty.
    Assessment criterion Marks
    Two correctly saved locations 2
    Correct decimal-degree readings 2
    Correct UTM zone and coordinates 2
    Verified KMZ and screenshot 2
    CRS explanation and limitations 2
    Total 10
    Challenge

    Reflection: Agricultural measurements

    Why does it matter whether a field boundary comes from rough imagery interpretation or a surveyed GNSS boundary?

    A GIS can calculate an area from either, but the reliability of that number depends on the quality of the boundary, not just the CRS. Digitizing unclear image edges may introduce substantial error, whereas a well-designed survey can provide more defensible field measurements.

    9. Sources and media credits

    • EPSG:4326 — WGS 84.
    • EPSG:32638 — WGS 84 / UTM zone 38N.
    • QGIS guidance on coordinate reference systems.
    • Google KML documentation.

    All three illustrations above are original works of their credited third-party creators and have not been AI-generated or modified for this lesson. The first is CC0; the second and third are individually licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Their respective image licenses remain in effect independently from the CC BY 4.0 license for the course’s original text.

    Both videos are embedded from their creators’ YouTube channels, not copied or re-uploaded. YouTube videos are not assumed to be open-license material; if an embedded player is blocked, open its linked video page.

    Key Points
    • GIS = geometry + attributes + a valid CRS.
    • Latitude and longitude are angles, generally expressed in degrees.
    • EPSG:4326 is a geographic WGS 84 CRS.
    • EPSG:32638 is projected WGS 84 / UTM Zone 38N, useful for local metric mapping around Sulaymaniyah.
    • Changing coordinate display formats is not reprojection.
    • Save field observations with appropriate source, accuracy and CRS information.

    Content from Lecture 3: GPS, GNSS, and Agricultural Positioning

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    GNSS is the umbrella term for satellite navigation systems; GPS is one constellation. Position accuracy depends on signal geometry, sky visibility, reflections, equipment and any corrections. Ordinary phone positions are not equivalent to validated RTK survey data. The supplied CSV contains synthetic teaching coordinates, not measurements.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS 3.x and spreadsheet
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Download the synthetic GNSS CSV linked below.
    2. Open QGIS and select Layer > Add Layer > Add Delimited Text Layer.
    3. Select longitude as X, latitude as Y, with CRS EPSG:4326.
    4. Open the points’ attribute table and inspect the quality_label field.
    5. Style point markers by quality_label and produce a screenshot.
    6. Export the layer to GeoPackage and save the QGIS project.

    Downloadable learning data

    GNSS practice CSV

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Why could GNSS positions under trees vary between observations?

    Poor sky view, multipath reflections and satellite geometry can affect positions. Use open sky, repeat observations, and appropriate correction equipment when higher accuracy is required.

    3. Student assignment

    Required submission: Categorized point map, GeoPackage, QGIS project, and comparison of phone GNSS versus RTK.

    Use a descriptive filename beginning with Lecture03. Explain what the map or output shows, give its coordinate reference system and units when relevant, and mention at least one uncertainty.

    Marking criterion Marks
    Correct preparation of data, location and CRS 2
    Practical workflow completed accurately 3
    Clear map or specified output files 2
    Agricultural interpretation and limitations 2
    Organized, reproducible submission 1
    Total 10
    Challenge

    Reflection

    Describe one agricultural application of this technique in Sulaymaniyah. Which extra evidence or checking would be needed before applying the result on an actual farm?

    Name the agricultural objective, describe the location-based information needed, and specify data quality, field validation and operational constraints. Avoid making real management recommendations from synthetic datasets.

    4. Further reading

    • Reference 1
    Key Points
    • Document data origin, accuracy, CRS, units and dates.
    • Check the validity of measurements, analyses and map exports.
    • Treat synthetic examples as demonstrations only.
    • Keep projects and supporting data together for reproducibility.

    Content from Lecture 4: Google Earth Pro for Farm Mapping

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    A point denotes a place, a line a path, and a polygon an area. KML stores geographic features; KMZ packages KML with related resources. Image-digitized farm boundaries are approximate: imagery date, unclear field edges, placement and digitizing decisions all influence accuracy. They are not legal surveys.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: Google Earth Pro
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Navigate to a cultivated area near Sulaymaniyah.
    2. Make a folder called Lecture04_Farm in Google Earth Pro Places.
    3. Use Add > Polygon to digitize one training field and name it Field_A.
    4. Use Add > Path for a track and Add > Placemark for an observation.
    5. Inspect the polygon’s approximate area and perimeter under Properties > Measurements.
    6. Save the complete folder as Lecture04_Farm.kmz and reopen it to verify.
    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Two students obtain different areas for the same field. Does that prove that the field changed?

    No. They may have traced different edges or used different imagery; assess positional and digitizing uncertainty before making that claim.

    3. Student assignment

    Required submission: KMZ with a polygon, path and placemark; screenshot; approximate area and three uncertainties.

    Use a descriptive filename beginning with Lecture04. Explain what the map or output shows, give its coordinate reference system and units when relevant, and mention at least one uncertainty.

    Content from Lecture 5: Google My Maps and Field Data

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    Google My Maps can import a coordinate table, group features into layers, style them by attributes and share a map. Clear coordinate names, units and descriptions are essential. Public map sharing can expose sensitive real locations, so use synthetic or approved data in training.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: Google My Maps
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Download the synthetic GNSS CSV linked below.
    2. Visit Google My Maps, create a map and name it L05 Agricultural Observations.
    3. Import the CSV into a new layer, selecting latitude and longitude as location fields.
    4. Use point_id for the feature title and style by quality_label.
    5. Inspect two marker descriptions and add a map-level note that data are synthetic.
    6. Export as KML/KMZ if the available interface permits, and check privacy settings.

    Downloadable learning data

    GNSS practice CSV

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Why is it safer to label spreadsheet columns latitude and longitude rather than simply x and y?

    Explicit coordinate labels prevent import errors and help students recognize coordinate order and spatial reference.

    Required submission: My Maps screenshot, exported map if supported, and a short privacy statement.

    Content from Lecture 6: Introduction to QGIS

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    QGIS is an open-source spatial analysis program. A .qgz project generally stores layer references, styles and layouts, not necessarily the datasets themselves. GeoPackage can store spatial layers. A CSV with latitudes and longitudes must be imported with its correct CRS.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS 3.x
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Create folders data, project and outputs in a Lecture06 workspace.
    2. Download the synthetic soil CSV linked below into data.
    3. In QGIS find the Layers, Browser, Map Canvas and Processing panels.
    4. Add the CSV using Delimited Text, X longitude, Y latitude, CRS EPSG:4326.
    5. Open the attribute table to inspect soil_ph and nitrogen_index.
    6. Export the layer to a GeoPackage and save project/L06.qgz.
    7. Reopen the saved project and confirm that the layer paths work.

    Downloadable learning data

    Soil practice CSV

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Why might a QGIS project show a missing-layer warning after copying only its .qgz file?

    The project references source files that were not copied or whose paths changed. Reconnect the layers or move the project with its source data.

    3. Student assignment

    Required submission: Working QGIS project, GeoPackage, screenshot, and explanation of source files versus projects.

    Use a descriptive filename beginning with Lecture06. Explain what the map or output shows, give its coordinate reference system and units when relevant, and mention at least one uncertainty.

    Marking criterion Marks
    Correct preparation of data, location and CRS 2
    Practical workflow completed accurately 3
    Clear map or specified output files 2
    Agricultural interpretation and limitations 2
    Organized, reproducible submission 1
    Total 10

    Reflection

    Describe one agricultural application of this technique in Sulaymaniyah. Which extra evidence or checking would be needed before applying the result on an actual farm?

    Name the agricultural objective, describe the location-based information needed, and specify data quality, field validation and operational constraints. Avoid making real management recommendations from synthetic datasets.

    Content from Lecture 7: Vector Layers and Agricultural Mapping

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    Vector layers represent point, line and polygon features with attributes. A polygon can store a field boundary and crop type; a line can store an irrigation route. For local planar area calculations use a suitable metric CRS, such as EPSG:32638 in Sulaymaniyah, rather than degree-squared coordinates.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS 3.x
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Load the soil points from Lecture 6 into a QGIS project.
    2. Create a new GeoPackage polygon layer named farm_fields in EPSG:32638.
    3. Digitize a training field polygon around the observation points.
    4. Add text attributes field_id and crop.
    5. Create a line layer representing a hypothetical irrigation route.
    6. Calculate the polygon area in hectares from square metres divided by 10,000.
    7. Create a print layout with title, legend and scale bar and export PDF.
    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Why cannot a planar area measured in squared degrees be directly reported in hectares?

    Degrees are angular units, not fixed metres. Reproject to a suitable metric CRS or use an appropriate geodesic area algorithm before converting to hectares.

    3. Student assignment

    Required submission: GeoPackage, area attribute, and final map PDF with legend and units.

    Use a descriptive filename beginning with Lecture07. Explain what the map or output shows, give its coordinate reference system and units when relevant, and mention at least one uncertainty.

    Practical workflow completed accurately 3
    Clear map or specified output files 2
    Agricultural interpretation and limitations 2
    Organized, reproducible submission 1

    Content from Lecture 8: Raster Data and Spatial Analysis

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    Rasters store values in cells. Cell size, extent, NoData, CRS and acquisition method determine what analyses are possible. A DEM represents terrain elevations; slope can be derived from it, but resolution and vertical accuracy must be appropriate to the intended farm decision.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS 3.x
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Obtain a permitted sample georeferenced DEM and record its source.
    2. Load the raster with Layer > Add Layer > Add Raster Layer.
    3. In Layer Properties > Information, note CRS, dimensions, cell size, units and NoData.
    4. Display the DEM with grayscale or pseudocolor symbology.
    5. Run an available Processing Toolbox Slope algorithm and inspect its parameters.
    6. Compare the DEM and slope layers and export a map with source attribution.
    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Can a 30-metre DEM reliably represent a narrow 20-centimetre-wide irrigation furrow?

    No. The feature is far below raster cell size; increased display sharpness cannot recover absent spatial detail.

    3. Student assignment

    Required submission: Raster metadata table, original DEM plus slope QGIS project, and interpreted map.

    Use a descriptive filename beginning with Lecture08. Explain what the map or output shows, give its coordinate reference system and units when relevant, and mention at least one uncertainty.

    Content from Lecture 9: Soil Sampling and Fertility Mapping

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    Georeferenced sampling connects laboratory observations to field locations. Styling observed points is not the same as predicting between points. Interpolation uses assumptions that should be validated. The course’s soil measurements are fictional, and nitrogen_index is not calibrated for fertilizer prescriptions.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS 3.x
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Import the synthetic soil CSV into QGIS using X longitude and Y latitude, EPSG:4326.
    2. Symbolize observations using Graduated style by soil_ph.
    3. Label a few sample_id values and inspect nitrogen_index.
    4. Optionally run IDW interpolation for soil_ph using QGIS Processing.
    5. Compare the modeled surface with the original observed points.
    6. Export a map labeled SYNTHETIC TRAINING DATA – NOT FOR FARM RECOMMENDATIONS.

    Downloadable learning data

    Soil practice CSV

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Why can an interpolation raster look detailed despite only twelve sample observations?

    Many rendered pixels are model estimates, not additional observations. Sampling density, method and uncertainty limit reliable interpretation.

    Required submission: pH sample map, optional IDW raster, project and limitations paragraph.

    Content from Lecture 10: Remote Sensing for Agriculture

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    Remote sensing collects information without direct contact. Spectral bands record radiation at different wavelengths, and satellite imagery differs in spatial, temporal, spectral and radiometric resolution. Cloud, shadows, seasonal crop stage and soil background influence interpretation.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS and satellite imagery browser
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Open Copernicus Browser and navigate to an agricultural area near Sulaymaniyah.
    2. Choose a crop-season date and inspect cloud coverage.
    3. Identify satellite source, product type, acquisition date and pixel size.
    4. Examine true-color and false-color displays if available.
    5. Download a permitted georeferenced sample if possible, or document the browser visualization.
    6. Identify two agricultural patterns and explain alternative reasons for each.
    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Do different colors on satellite imagery prove one field is diseased?

    No. Different crops, growth stage, soil, irrigation, atmospheric effects or image stretching can cause differences; verify with field evidence.

    Content from Lecture 11: Satellite Imagery and NDVI

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red), using comparable near-infrared and red reflectance values. NDVI is frequently between -1 and 1 but is not a direct measurement of disease, nitrogen requirement or crop yield. Clouds, soil background, zero denominators and acquisition date must be addressed.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: Spreadsheet and optionally QGIS Raster Calculator
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Download the synthetic NDVI pixel CSV linked below.
    2. Add an NDVI column to a spreadsheet.
    3. For valid rows compute (nir - red) / (nir + red).
    4. Mark denominator-zero rows as invalid instead of dividing by zero.
    5. Compare vegetation, bare soil and water teaching examples.
    6. Optionally use QGIS Raster Calculator on aligned red and NIR reflectance rasters.
    7. Summarize two limitations of NDVI-based agricultural interpretation.

    Downloadable learning data

    NDVI practice CSV

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Calculate NDVI for NIR 0.62 and Red 0.18.

    (0.62 − 0.18)/(0.62 + 0.18) = 0.44/0.80 = 0.55.

    3. Student assignment

    Required submission: Completed NDVI spreadsheet, optional map, and interpretation of two pixel values.

    Use a descriptive filename beginning with Lecture11. Explain what the map or output shows, give its coordinate reference system and units when relevant, and mention at least one uncertainty.

    Content from Lecture 12: Drone Mapping and Crop Monitoring

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    An orthomosaic joins corrected overlapping drone images into a georeferenced image. Ground sampling distance (GSD) describes ground pixel footprint; it does not equal position accuracy. Mapping quality also depends on GNSS, alignment, ground control, processing and terrain. This class does not require an actual drone flight.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS; optional permitted orthomosaic
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Obtain a permitted demonstration orthomosaic or other georeferenced sample imagery.
    2. Load imagery into QGIS and inspect CRS, pixel size and data origin.
    3. Create a scouting point GeoPackage with issue_type and notes attributes.
    4. Digitize three observation points at visible surface features.
    5. Categorize observations and prepare a map layout with scale and legend.
    6. Write a ground verification plan, and identify local permissions required before any real flight.
    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    If orthomosaic ground pixel size is 3 cm, must its mapping accuracy be 3 cm?

    No. Pixel footprint is different from horizontal positional accuracy. Alignment, control points and GNSS quality all matter.

    3. Student assignment

    Required submission: Scouting points GeoPackage, annotated orthomosaic map and safety/verification plan.

    Use a descriptive filename beginning with Lecture12. Explain what the map or output shows, give its coordinate reference system and units when relevant, and mention at least one uncertainty.

    Content from Lecture 13: Management Zones and Variable-Rate Technology

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    Management zones are hypotheses about areas with similar management needs. Multiple seasons, soils, yields and field checks are desirable. Variable-rate application needs agronomically justified rates, compatible equipment, calibration and monitoring. These synthetic records must NEVER be used as prescriptions.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS and spreadsheet
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Import synthetic soil and yield CSV datasets as two QGIS point layers.
    2. Style soil pH and yield values separately using graduated categories.
    3. Compare their locations and patterns without asserting causal relationships.
    4. Digitize two or three conceptual polygons into a new management_zones layer.
    5. Add zone_id, evidence and confidence attributes.
    6. Prepare a map labeled CONCEPTUAL ZONES ONLY – NOT AN APPLICATION PRESCRIPTION.
    7. Describe what data and calibration would be required for real-world variable-rate applications.

    Downloadable learning data

    Soil CSV and yield CSV

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Can one coincident high yield and high nitrogen-index value establish a fertilizer rate?

    No. A short synthetic dataset cannot determine response, cause or suitable rate. Local crop requirements, representative testing, agronomic calibration and operational validation are necessary.

    3. Student assignment

    Required submission: Conceptual zone GeoPackage, two thematic maps, and a VRT safeguards note.

    Use a descriptive filename beginning with Lecture13. Explain what the map or output shows, give its coordinate reference system and units when relevant, and mention at least one uncertainty.

    Content from Lecture 14: Final Practical GIS Project

    Last updated on 2026-10-26 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What agricultural problem does this technology address?
    • What information and software are needed to use it responsibly?
    • What evidence is required before making a field-management decision?

    Objectives

    After this lecture students should be able to explain the topic, complete its practical workflow, preserve the source data and interpret its limitations.

    1. Principles

    The final project should answer a modest, explicit agricultural question through a reproducible GIS workflow. Distinguish observed from synthetic or modeled information. Results need an identifiable source, CRS, scale, analysis method, limitations and data attribution.

    Callout

    Course context

    University: University of Sulaimani
    Software: QGIS and optional Google Earth Pro
    Study region: Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq
    Practice time: Approximately 60 minutes

    All supplied course CSV data are synthetic educational examples, not real field measurements.

    2. Practical exercise — step by step

    1. Choose one agricultural mapping question and write a one-sentence objective.
    2. Create structured data, project, outputs and documentation folders.
    3. Use at least two geographic layers including a point layer and a polygon or raster.
    4. Record source, license, coordinate reference system and dates for each input.
    5. Carry out a suitable spatial operation: area, buffer, thematic comparison or carefully labeled interpolation.
    6. Export one readable final map PDF with legend, scale, title and attribution.
    7. Prepare a 300–500-word report covering purpose, methods, results and limitations.
    8. Reopen the project from the submission folder to test reproducibility.
    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    How should a student describe a result based solely on synthetic demonstration data?

    Clearly label it a teaching demonstration and refrain from asserting real field yield, nutrient levels, or management benefits.
